metadata.title: Prolonged stepwise fever in a 19-year-old student in Karachi
metadata.author: seed

patient.name: Bilal Ahmed
patient.personality: Polite, a little tired and run down
patient.communication_style: Answers clearly but looks unwell and lethargic

history.chief_complaint: Fever for about a week that keeps climbing higher each day

history_of_presenting_illness.onset: Gradual over 7 days, stepwise rising fever (worse in the evenings)
history_of_presenting_illness.abdomen: Vague central abdominal discomfort and bloating
history_of_presenting_illness.bowel: Mild constipation initially, now loose stools
history_of_presenting_illness.associated: Headache, poor appetite, marked tiredness, dry cough
history_of_presenting_illness.exposure: Regularly eats from roadside food stalls; drinks unfiltered tap water

family_history: A cousin had typhoid last month
social_history: Lives in a densely populated area of Karachi

abdomen.rose_spots: A few faint rose-coloured spots on the trunk

laboratory.name: Blood Culture
laboratory.clinical_significance: Gold standard; sensitivities guide therapy (XDR typhoid is prevalent in Sindh)

laboratory.name: Widal Test
laboratory.clinical_significance: Suggestive but not confirmatory; culture is preferred

imaging.name: Abdominal Ultrasound
imaging.result: Mild splenomegaly, no abscess or free fluid

bedside.name: Malaria Rapid Diagnostic Test
bedside.clinical_significance: Reasonable to exclude malaria in any febrile patient here

diagnosis.explanation: A week of stepwise fever with relative bradycardia, abdominal symptoms, splenomegaly, rose spots and leucopenia, with Salmonella Typhi on blood culture, confirms enteric fever — and the XDR pattern is important in the Pakistani setting.

emergency_management: Empirical antibiotics guided by local XDR typhoid resistance (azithromycin or a carbapenem such as meropenem; ceftriaxone often ineffective in XDR)
Monitor for complications (GI bleeding, intestinal perforation)
follow_up: Safe water and food hygiene advice

items.description: Characterised the fever pattern and duration
Started appropriate antibiotics (consider local XDR resistance)
Explained the diagnosis, prevention and hygiene

pearls: Relative bradycardia (Faget sign) and leucopenia are clues to enteric fever.
Blood culture is the gold standard; the Widal test is only supportive.
pitfalls: Using ceftriaxone empirically where XDR Salmonella Typhi is prevalent (much of Pakistan).
Missing perforation in a patient whose pain suddenly worsens.
references: WHO typhoid guidance; Pakistan XDR typhoid advisories
learning_objectives: Choose antibiotics in the context of local XDR resistance.
